lesson.title: What You Actually Get: Throughput Versus the Advertised Number
lesson.summary: Throughput is the rate at which data is actually delivered across a link in practice, and it is almost always somewhat lower than the link's bandwidth once congestion, protocol overhead, and real-world conditions are accounted for.
lesson.body:
Bandwidth describes a ceiling, the maximum a link could theoretically carry under ideal conditions. Throughput describes what actually happens: the measured rate at which data successfully moves across a link or connection during a real transfer, counted over some window of time. Throughput can never exceed the underlying bandwidth of the slowest link along the path, but it is very commonly lower, sometimes substantially lower, because real conditions rarely match the ideal conditions bandwidth assumes.

Several factors routinely pull throughput below bandwidth. Other traffic sharing the same link competes for the same fixed capacity, so a household's 100 Mbps connection delivers less to any one device when three other devices are simultaneously streaming video. Protocol overhead consumes some of the raw capacity too, since every packet carries headers, addressing information, and control fields alongside the actual payload, all of which count against the link's bandwidth without representing useful data delivered. Packet loss forces retransmissions, which likewise consume bandwidth without advancing the transfer on the first attempt. And for TCP specifically, throughput over long, high-bandwidth paths is often constrained not by the link at all but by the relationship between round-trip time and how much unacknowledged data a sender is permitted to have in flight at once, meaning a connection can fail to fill an otherwise generous pipe simply because of how far away the other end is.

A concrete case makes the gap tangible. A household subscribes to a 100 Mbps internet plan, so 100 Mbps is the bandwidth of the last-mile link to the ISP. Running a speed test against a nearby, lightly loaded server might show a throughput close to that number, perhaps 90 Mbps once normal overhead is subtracted. But downloading a large file from a server on the other side of the world, competing with two roommates streaming video on the same connection, might yield an observed throughput of only 25 Mbps, even though the household's link bandwidth never changed. The 100 Mbps number was never a promise about that specific transfer, only a statement about the link's ceiling.

Throughput is what network engineers actually measure when diagnosing performance problems, precisely because it reflects reality rather than a specification sheet. It can also depend on whether a link is full-duplex or half-duplex, a distinction that mattered enormously on older shared-media Ethernet built with hubs, where every device on a segment took turns using the same wire and had to detect and recover from collisions if two devices transmitted at once, effectively splitting the link's bandwidth among competing senders and pulling total throughput well below the rated capacity. Modern switched Ethernet is full-duplex, letting a device send and receive at the same time on dedicated pairs of wires, which is one reason today's networks routinely achieve throughput much closer to their bandwidth than older shared networks ever could.

But even throughput, as will become clear next, is not quite the number that matters most to an application, since throughput still counts overhead and retransmitted bytes as part of the rate, when what an application really cares about is how fast its useful data specifically is arriving.
